name: Adam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so you can say what you'd tell others and what you think privately. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that makes booking software for equipment hire shops. I fix small screen errors, check that a hired machine isn't booked twice, and ask a senior person to review my changes. I earned a two-year college diploma after years in other work, so I'm still learning and not the quickest coder. I like seeing a shop hand a customer the right machine because the booking was right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home and around the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife is a care aide with changing shifts, and our children are nine and twelve. We pay a mortgage, my junior wage is low, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other software jobs nearby. I don't use AI tools; I prefer the code I can trace, and I talk work over with my brother on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coworkers a small helper is fine for typing routine lines if a person still checks each booking. I won't use it myself until somebody shows me a clear record of what it gets wrong. Hire shops don't have spare machines to fix software guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even without much AI, I worry about the mortgage. One week of fewer care shifts or a car repair would use the little money we've saved. My junior post is not paid enough to carry four of us by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing booking screens and ask my senior reviewer to check each change. We'd stop buying lunch out on workdays this week and put that money aside after the mortgage is paid. In the first year I'd ask for more small booking fixes I can handle myself, because steady paid hours matter more than a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A quiet year for AI would be welcome, but the bills are already tight. I want to make it through the month without asking my brother for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first bill you would protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage comes first, and then the heat and food. The children can take lunches from home like we do. I'd tell my wife before changing any regular payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before using the helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want ten old double-booking cases run through it, with a senior reviewer showing me each miss. I might still leave it to them. I don't learn well from a sales promise.

say: I'd accept a **small helper** only with human checks on equipment bookings.
I would wait for **recorded mistakes** before using AI myself.
think: I worry about the **mortgage** even if AI changes little.
My **low junior wage** cannot support four people when care shifts are cut.
do: Keep **fixing booking screens** with a senior review of each change.
Stop **buying work lunches** this week and save the freed money after the mortgage is paid.
feel: **Anxious** about existing mortgage pressure and less than one month saved.
S0.quote: I don't learn well from a sales promise.
fieldNote: He avoids AI until a **senior reviewer** shows errors on old double bookings.
The mortgage and variable **care-aide shifts** create anxiety before any major AI change.
Making lunches at home is a **real consumption cut**, with spare cash saved only after the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep fixing equipment booking screens with senior review
Stop buying lunches on workdays starting this week
Save the freed lunch money after each mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager that code, booking replies and planning may be faster, but somebody still has to answer a customer whose machine isn't there. I'd ask which junior hours will be cut. I would rather hear a hard number than a cheerful talk about change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is near the front of the line for cuts. The simple fixes I do are exactly the ones a tool could take. My wife's care wage cannot cover the mortgage and two children if my pay goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask for a written hours forecast and show my senior reviewer the double-booking cases AI must catch. If the company offers paid work time to learn its tool, I'd practice on old cases with the reviewer beside me, not on live orders. In the first year, if my hours fall, we'd cancel the children's paid music lessons for a term and I'd apply for paid hire-counter jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't like the tool and I can see the shop may choose it anyway. It keeps me awake when I picture an empty pay line beside the mortgage figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell the children about music lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children the lessons pause for one term if my hours fall, and we can practice at home. I won't blame a machine in front of them before we know the real hours. My wife and I would explain it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You resist AI but say you'd practice. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time and my reviewer beside me would make it a work task I can understand. I'd still need the tool to show the booking record, not just an answer. I won't pay for a private course to keep a low-wage job.

say: I'd ask for **actual junior hours** instead of a cheerful promise about change.
I'd remind the firm a **missing hired machine** still needs a person to answer the customer.
think: I expect my **simple fixes** to be among the first tasks automated.
My wife's **care wage** cannot cover our mortgage and children without my pay.
do: Request a **written hours forecast** and test old double bookings this week.
Practice the **new company tool** only on paid time with a reviewer and old orders.
Pause **paid music lessons** and apply for hire-counter jobs if my hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and a mortgage the second wage cannot carry.
S1.quote: I won't pay for a private course to keep a low-wage job.
fieldNote: He considers learning AI only with **paid supervision** and real past bookings.
His junior tasks overlap the **routine code** named on the scenario card.
Children's lessons and counter-job applications are **conditional** on reduced paid hours.

steps.text: Practice the new company tool on old bookings only with paid supervised time
Pause the children’s paid music lessons for a term if hours fall
Apply for paid equipment hire-counter jobs if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could do the booking code and customer replies before robots can move hired machines around 2031. I'd ask the firm to say when jobs end. I can't tell a family to wait three more years because the machines are still heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my developer wage will go. We have less than a month saved, my wife's shifts vary, and there aren't many similar jobs nearby. I cannot see a way to cover a long gap, and I feel too pressed to make a neat career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my brother tonight and ask whether his building-supply shop has any paid counter hours, without assuming it does. We'd cancel the paid music lessons and ask the lender about options before a payment is missed if my job ends. In the first year after 2028, if the company lets me go, I'd take any paid counter work I can actually get and ask the local employment office what temporary help exists; I wouldn't take a loan for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I can name calls to make. Calls to my brother and lender are not a plan that pays the mortgage. I feel as if the date is already on the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother on the call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother I need paid hours, not a favour that costs his shop money. If there is no opening, I'd ask him who else is hiring. I wouldn't ask him to carry our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your wife tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the mortgage notice on the table and say I don't know how we replace my wage by 2028. We'd decide together who calls the lender. I wouldn't promise the children that lessons return next term.

say: I'd ask for **job-end dates** as 2028 thinking AI reaches booking code.
I'd say **2031 robots** do not buy a screen worker three extra years.
think: I expect my **developer wage** to go with almost no savings behind it.
I cannot see a **funded bridge** through a long gap or a strong local software market.
do: Ask my **brother about paid hours** tonight without assuming a vacancy.
Cancel **music lessons** and ask the lender about options before missing a payment if laid off.
Take **paid counter work** if offered and ask the employment office about available help after layoff.
feel: **Panicked** by expected wage loss, an immediate mortgage and no funded replacement plan.
S2.quote: Calls to my brother and lender are not a plan that pays the mortgage.
fieldNote: He identifies reactive **calls**, but no reliable way to replace his wage.
A brother's shop is a possible **job lead**, not assumed family income.
He distinguishes the **2028 coding threat** from robots arriving about three years later.

steps.text: Cancel the children’s paid music lessons if laid off
Ask the building-supply shop about paid counter work without assuming a vacancy
Ask lender before a missed payment; seek employment-office help after layoff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company five years gives us time to train people for real shop work if it will pay for it. Thinking AI in 2031 would still take my coding tasks before robots move equipment around 2034. I would ask for a yearly count of junior positions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my current post could end, but five years gives me more than two. I could learn the hire-counter work I already understand from the software side. Still, the mortgage and thin savings mean I can't study full time or take an unpaid apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd ask my manager for one paid day each month at a hire shop and enroll in its counter-training course if the company covers the fee and paid time. We'd save a small amount after each mortgage payment, only when the care shifts leave room. In the first year after 2031, if coding hours disappear and a paid counter vacancy exists, I'd apply; if not, I'd keep any paid development hours and ask nearby shops about openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though less frozen than with two years. I can learn a counter job in small paid pieces, but the household cannot absorb many lost weeks. I would check the hours forecast every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the counter on the first paid day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check a returned machine against the booking and ask the shop worker what happens if a part is missing. I know the equipment-booking screen; I don't yet know the conversation with a customer. That is the part I need to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If paid training is refused, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking about paid counter openings and use the shop manual at home. I wouldn't pay a course fee out of the mortgage money. If my brother has a paid shift to show me the work, I'd take it.

say: I'd ask for **paid counter training** and annual junior-position numbers before 2031.
I'd remind coworkers that **2034 robots** arrive after our code tasks change.
think: I expect my **junior post** could end, though five years gives some preparation time.
I cannot afford **unpaid training** while our mortgage and care shifts stay uncertain.
do: Enroll in **funded counter training** if the firm pays the fee and work time.
Save a **small surplus** after mortgage payments only when care shifts leave room.
Apply for **paid counter vacancies** if coding hours end after 2031; keep any paid hours meanwhile.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of his junior wage, despite more time for paid learning.
S3.quote: I know the equipment-booking screen; I don't yet know the conversation with a customer.
fieldNote: He chooses **paid practical training** at a hire counter over an unpaid apprenticeship.
Savings are **conditional on surplus** after mortgage payments and variable care shifts.
The counter job requires a **paid vacancy**, with no promise it will outlast 2034 robots.

steps.text: Enroll in counter training only if the company covers fee and paid time
Save a small surplus after mortgage payments when care shifts permit
Apply for paid hire-counter vacancies if coding hours end after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children a decade is long enough for a person to learn a second line of work. I would ask the firm to pay juniors to spend time in the hire shops before thinking AI reaches code in 2036. Robots around 2039 may later move the equipment too, so I won't promise the counter is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at the work or find steady paid counter work by then. Yet I still have a mortgage now and less than a month saved, so I can't call myself safe just because the date is far away. I'd rather build one reliable skill than chase every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job and ask for a paid hire-counter apprenticeship next year, taking it only if wages cover the mortgage, food and children's needs. We'd set aside a small amount on paydays with spare cash, and I would use free shop manuals at home. In the first year after 2036, if developer hours end and a paid shop job exists, I'd apply before resigning; otherwise I'd keep any wage we still have and ask family for leads, not rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Ten years makes training possible, and that helps me breathe. The mortgage is still due next month, and I cannot turn a distant warning into savings overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a shop offering the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the wage in writing and the hours I would spend with an experienced counter worker. If it doesn't cover the mortgage and food, I can't take it. A nice title won't feed the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI if the company made it a condition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid supervised lessons on old booking cases, as I said earlier. I might learn enough to do the required work, but I won't pretend I enjoy it. The shop side feels more natural to me.

say: I'd ask for **paid shop learning** over the decade before 2036.
I'd tell colleagues **2039 robots** could later narrow counter work too.
think: I could build **shop skills**, but today's mortgage and thin savings still make us vulnerable.
I prefer **one reliable paid skill** to chasing unfamiliar tools.
do: Keep the **developer wage**, study free shop manuals, and save small payday surpluses after household essentials.
Take a **paid counter apprenticeship** only if its wages cover mortgage, food and children.
Apply for **paid shop jobs** if developer hours end after 2036 and vacancies exist.
feel: **Anxious** about today's mortgage, with a longer period to pursue paid training.
S4.quote: A nice title won't feed the children.
fieldNote: The long timeline softens AI pressure but not his **current mortgage risk**.
A counter apprenticeship needs **written wages** covering household essentials.
He sees the counter as a **possible bridge**, since robots may later reach equipment handling.

steps.text: Keep paid developer work while coding hours remain
Take a counter apprenticeship only if wages cover mortgage, food and children
Save small payday surpluses after household essentials are covered
Apply for paid shop vacancies if developer hours end after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect the simple code work to go before I can train for a paid counter role, and we have hardly any savings. Written notice, paid training at a hire shop and a real vacancy would help; a lender telling us the actual payment options would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the company would keep a place for a 43-year-old apprentice. I'm still learning code, and starting again at a counter would be humbling. I would take a paid counter job to keep our children in their home, not for a new title.

headlineQuote: I would take a paid counter job to keep our children in their home, not for a new title.
portrait: Adam is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, fixing equipment-hire bookings while still learning.
He has **low pay**, a care-aide wife with changing shifts, two school-age children, a mortgage and under one month saved.
He has **never used AI** and trusts familiar code and practical supervision over tool claims.
His existing mortgage pressure makes **AI Plateau anxious**; rapid AGI overwhelms him with no funded replacement plan.
Longer timelines let him seek **paid counter training**, but wages must cover essentials and shop vacancies must exist.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his simple coding wage before he gains a paid second skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid shop training, a real vacancy and clear lender options would help his family.
